hints: Look for carbon atoms joined to four different atoms or groups, focus on the two carbons in the centre that each carry N, H, C=O and a carbon side chain.
walkthrough:
Recall what counts as chiral**
Think of a chiral carbon as a carbon with four completely different groups attached. If any two groups are the same, it cannot be chiral. So you can ignore all $\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_3$, $\text{C(CH}_3)_3$ and $\text{C=O}$ carbons straight away.

Check the two central backbone carbons**
In Fig. 8.1 there are two carbons that each carry H, N and C=O plus a different carbon chain. The left one carries $\text{NH(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(CH}_3)_3)$, $\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$, H and $\text{C(=O)NH}$, all four different. The right one carries $\text{NHC(=O)}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$, H and $\text{C(=O)OCH}_3$, all four different. No other carbon has four different groups, so the total is 2.

hints: Scan Fig. 8.1 from left to right and label each N and each C=O separately, remembering that C=O joined to N is different from C=O joined to O.
Remember that a nitrogen joined to carbon atoms only is an amine, while a nitrogen joined directly to C=O is an amide, and a C=O joined to OH is different from C=O joined to OR.
walkthrough:
Sort out the nitrogen groups**
You have two nitrogens. The one on the right is $\text{-C(=O)-NH-CH-}$, a carbonyl directly attached to N. That is an amide. The one on the left is $\text{-CH}_2\text{-NH-CH-}$, nitrogen attached to two carbons and one H with no carbonyl. That is a secondary amine.

Sort out the carbonyl groups**
You have three $\text{C=O}$ groups. The bottom left $\text{-C(=O)-OH}$ is a carboxylic acid. The top middle $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ is the amide carbonyl already counted. The bottom right $\text{-C(=O)-OCH}_3$ is a carbonyl joined to an alkoxy group, so it is an ester.

Put the full list together**
Excluding the arene ring already given, neotame contains four other functional groups: secondary amine, amide, carboxylic acid and ester.
Final answer: amide, amine (secondary amine), ester and carboxylic acid / carboxyl

hints: Think about what hot aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ does to linkages made by condensation, such as $\text{-CONH-}$ and $\text{-COOR}$.
Think about what $\text{NaOH}$ does to an acidic proton, such as the $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ proton, even without breaking a carbon skeleton.
walkthrough:
Spot the bonds that water can split**
Hot $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ breaks condensation linkages by adding water across them. Neotame has one amide linkage $\text{-C(=O)-NH-}$ in the middle and one methyl ester $\text{-C(=O)-OCH}_3$ on the right. Both undergo alkaline hydrolysis to give carboxylate salts plus an amine and methanol.

Spot the simple proton transfer**
The $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ group on the left is already a carboxylic acid. It does not need bond breaking in the carbon skeleton, it simply donates $\text{H}^+$ to $\text{OH}^-$ to form $\text{-CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+$ plus water. That is a classic acid-base or neutralisation reaction.

Final answer: 1 hydrolysis (alkaline hydrolysis of amide and ester)
2 acid-base / neutralisation (of carboxylic acid to form carboxylate)

hints: Mark the two cleavage points in Fig. 8.1, the central amide C-N bond and the ester C-OR bond, to see that the molecule splits into three carbon fragments.

Remember that with excess hot $\text{NaOH}$, every $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ and every new $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ formed by hydrolysis exists as $\text{-CO}_2^-\text{Na}^+$, while amines remain as free $\text{-NH-}$ or $\text{-NH}_2$.
Check the small alcohol fragment from the methyl ester, it contains only one carbon joined to OH.
walkthrough:
Cut the molecule at the hydrolysable links**
Draw a line through the central amide $\text{C(=O)-NH}$ bond and through the ester $\text{C(=O)-OCH}_3$ bond. That gives you three skeletons: a left fragment with the bulky $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH-}$ plus aspartic acid backbone, a right fragment with the $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH-)-}$ backbone, and a $\text{CH}_3\text{O-}$ fragment.

Convert all acids to sodium salts**
Because excess $\text{NaOH}$ is used, write every carboxyl as $\text{C(=O)ONa}$ or $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$, not $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$. The left fragment therefore has two $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ groups, one original and one from the hydrolysed amide, and keeps its secondary amine $\text{NH}$. So it is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH(CH}_2\text{C(=O)ONa)C(=O)ONa}$.

Finish the amine and alcohol fragments**
The amide nitrogen stays with the right fragment as a free primary amine, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2)\text{C(=O)ONa}$. The ester $\text{OCH}_3$ picks up H to become methanol, $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$. Those are the three organic products, all drawn in their basic forms with no $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ remaining.

Final answer: Product 1 (left + middle aspartate fragment): $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NHCH(CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{Na})\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ containing two $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ groups and secondary amine NH
Product 2 (right phenylalanine fragment): $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CH(NH}_2)\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$ containing phenyl ring, $\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{CO}_2\text{Na}$
Product 3: $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ methanol
